utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom and behind the pillar. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Barney Thomas, Lorna Bolton, April Carter, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Thomas. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is today represented by Tina Drolec, Milos Androvic, Daniela Tasic, Gregor Guy-Smith, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Good afternoon, Mr. Dozo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, good afternoon. We shall continue where we left it off yesterday. I would like warn both you and myself to make a little pause after my question, do not start to answer immediately, and if you are going to give a lengthy answer, please, do it slowly for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First, I would like the court to produce a copy of 65 ter 9244, which is a map of Sarajevo. I would like us to try and pin-point for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and everybody in the courtroom the locations that we spoke about yesterday. Could the right-hand side of the map be blown up, even a bit more, please. Scroll up a little, please. Excellent, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, I would like to ask you about some of the locations that we have already mentioned. Are you able to find your bearings on the map?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would kindly ask you to encircle and mark by number 1, the location known as Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well, you don't have to make a circle, it's okay. Grdonj hill is something that you are familiar with, are you not? Could you please find it on this map and mark it by number 2.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Likewise, on Kobilja Glava, another hill top, can you mark that by putting number 3 next to it. Do you see it on the map?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kobilja Glava is a neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the neighbourhood called Barutana. Can you mark it by putting number 4 next to it.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that all the locations that you've just marked were part of the territory under the control of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BiH Army was in control of settlements, these are settlements and neighbourhoods. As soon as you leave a neighbourhood, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer controlled that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the settlements or neighbourhoods that we have just marked with the numbers were the neighbourhoods under the control of the BiH Army; am I right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These neighbourhoods were inhabited by its residents, by their residents, and that meant that these neighbourhoods were under the control of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the separation line was immediately outside of these neighbourhoods and that the area outside of those territories was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see Spicasta Stijena on this map?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then if that is the case, could you please mark by number 5 the location known as Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is on the elevation between Grdonj and Sedrenik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to you, Spicasta Stijena was under the control of the members of the Army of Republika Srpska; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D68, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for this document, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few more questions to bring this topic to an end, and I'm talking about the incident involving Mrs. Selmanovic. Yesterday, you said that after you had seen her after several months, and interviewed her, you did not show her the photos that were taken on the spot, on the day when the investigation was carried out?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Selmanovic was not shown any photos because the photos were filed with the MUP of the Sarajevo canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And with regard to the contents of the official note after your interview with her, she never explained to you where she was facing when she was hit?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't have the official note before me, but I believe that she said that she had gone out to fetch some fuel wood, and at that moment when she was gathering the fuel wood, she had been hit from Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce P1940, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, and this is approximately what the note has recorded, but I would like to avoid any confusion and I would like to ask you this: Did she tell you what her position was with regard to the house and with regard to Spicasta Stijena; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. Maybe my memory could be jogged by the official note, if that has indeed been recorded in the official note.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that from this record we cannot see how her body was positioned with regard to Spicasta Stijena at the moment she was hit and injured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to the second part of your testimony. Yesterday you testified and your statements also mention the events that preceded this incident, which we call Markale II in August 1995. As far as I could understand your statement and your testimony, the incidents that preceded the Markale II incident point to the fact that in your view that was a way to correct the sighting device in order to be able to hit the city marketplace, would that be the essence of your testimony and the statements that you provided regard to the events that preceded Markale II?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know which projectiles were used when the children and other people were injured in the previous incidents?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I believe that those were 120 millimetre mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you go to an onsite inspection, when you are a member of an inspection team, you do not receive subsequent information from the ballistics expert about the facts that he established?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when we marked the incidents that you described on the map, and I'm talking about the incidents that had preceded the Markale II incident, you could not tell us exactly when the incidents took place with regard to the Markale II incident?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I could not remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With regard to those events that you described in your testimony yesterday, you did not have any document about the inspection that was carried out with regard to these incidents, you did not have them on you. Did the Prosecution ever show them to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any documents on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor did not show you a single document that could be brought in connection with your description of any of these instance?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the first incident when the children were injured, that's how I'm going to define the incident because I don't remember the name of the street. I understand that according to your information, the projectile had come from the direction of Barica from the north?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the street called Geneta [phoen] Cikma Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the second incident, half an hour later when several shells fell in the vicinity of Markale, you obtained information that the projectiles had come from the direction of south from Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the direction of Racan and Lukavica or the slopes of Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record I would hold out to the court that this is an inaccurate depiction of the evidence from yesterday. The incident where the children were injured and the three separate shellings were on two different dates per the witness's evidence. So it's a misstatement of the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was very -- I did not deduce what he testified but what I learned from the proofing notes and from the sketch that he made, and that's how I am asking -- putting my question to the witness and that's how the witness understood me. I may have worded my question incorrectly. I just wanted to define the part of the his testimony provided yesterday that referred to the two incidents. He may not have spoken about the directions of the shells yesterday, but that's not how I put my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I seem to understand Madam Carter to be saying that there are two separate incidents which took place on two separate dates or times. The one in incident involving the children and the other three separate shellings. Yeah. They happened on two different dates. Now, I'm not quite sure whether you had suggested to the witness that they had happened on the same date, but I didn't pick that up, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may have been a mistake in the interpretation. The witness did say, and I repeated, that the two incidents were several days apart. There is no dispute about that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, if you look at page 7 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sorry. It's line 7, page 7, you say: "And the second incident, half an hour later, when several shells in the vicinity of Markale," suggesting that it's the same date. And that's, I think, what Madam Carter is objecting to. So they were separate dates, not half an hour later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was an interpretation mistake. I said the second incident that happened within the framework of half an hour, this is what I said, the interpreters may have not understood me. I'm trying very hard to speak slowly today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what do you mean by within the framework of half an hour? Aren't you suggesting the same date by so saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. The witness himself said that this happened a few days later within the scope of a half an hour on a different date, not on the date when the children were injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second incident which happened a few days later was the incident that involved shelling from the direction of Racan Lukavica according to your information?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This would be the southern part of Sarajevo in the opposite direction of the location that is Barica?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how far Lukavica is from Markale?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are saying, Mr. Dozo, that you were a member of the team which carried out onsite inspection on the two occasions: The first one when the children were hurt, and the second one a few days later when there was repeated shelling in various locations around Markale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And one of the shells, according to you, fell only some 30 metres away from Markale where the incident happened on the 28th, that's what you said, isn't that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it hit the building which housed the representative office of Konzum.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that if somebody wants to adjust the precision of a mortar, the mortar would have to remain at the same location and only the sights would have to be adjusted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to one shelling only, then that could be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can the sights be adjusted if a mortar is fired from different parts of town?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were so many artillery pieces that there was no need to transfer them from one line to another, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not participate in the onsite investigation. Do you know from which direction it was established that Markale II were fired on on the 2nd of August?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of projectile landed in that location?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that you were aware that one of the mandates of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo at the time was to make sure that no artillery pieces were fired from. They monitored the positions of both the BH Army and the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that representatives of UNPROFOR on the 28th of August, 1995, did not observe any artillery activity at the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, you told us that you were a member of the two teams that carried out the onsite investigations concerning the events that happened in the immediate vicinity of the Markale location, but you will agree with me that this is not within the competence of your police station?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Markale II, where the shell landed, that is not part of the jurisdiction of the Stari Grad police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But rather of the Centar police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was an onsite investigation 30 metres away from that location, so what were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third shell which hit the Konzum building landed on the territory of Stari Grad municipality in the immediate vicinity of the cathedral, some 30 metres away from the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the Markale market is at the border between the territories of two police stations?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dozo, would I be wrong if I were to say that when an investigating judge carries out an onsite investigation, as you described, and there were some such situations where you were a member of the team, the Stari Grad police station would only have the task of securing the area?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uniformed police officers are tasked with securing the site, whereas the team coming to assist at the onsite investigation is duty-bound to preserve the traces and to find pieces of the shell that had exploded in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you are saying that you actively participated in finding parts of the evidentiary material?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to all these onsite investigations concerning the shellings, and I asked you yesterday about the sniper incident, and you will confirm that you always arrived on the spot when victims had already been taken to hospital or unfortunately to the morgue, as the case may be, as a rule?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived only when we received information that something had happened. And in that time, the citizens or whoever happened to be there would try to help those people by taking them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you arrived on the spot, was the site already secured?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes it was and sometimes it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd asked for some specificity with regards to time. He has referred to shelling incidents, sniping incidents, and now this most recent question seems to be calling for a specific incidents, but I'm not clear which is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, I thought the question still related to general things. At line 25, page 11, he says: "In relation to all these onsite investigations concerning the shellings, and I asked you yesterday about the sniper incident, and you will confirm that you always arrived on the spot when victims had already been taken to hospital or unfortunately to the morgue as the case may be as a rule." The answer was: "We arrived only when we received information that something had happened. And in that time the citizens or whoever happened to be there would try to help those people." I'm not quite sure which --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: My concern actually came in in page 12, line 8, when it says: "When you arrived on the spot, was the site already secured," implying a specific point in time, as opposed to generalities before. That's why I didn't object to the initial portion, but seems to imply a specific time and place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think read in the context of the previous response, to me it sounds like it's still general. When you arrive at a spot, whatever spot it is, you find the place secured already. Anyway, Mr. Lukic, can you help us. Were you being specific to a specific place or were you being general?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was general, referring to the witness's experience with regard to onsite investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what is the task of those who are securing the spot before the and after the onsite investigation when an incident occurs, what do they do?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it's a case of shelling, the policemen on the ground, one or two of them were duty-bound to make sure that no one can enter, no citizens, members of the general public, can enter the area where the explosion had taken place unless someone had to be given first aid or transported to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your experience, in relation to the investigations you attended and the information you received when an incident happened, how much time would elapse from the point of time when an incident occurred, to the point of time when security was put in place?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would all depend on how intensive the shelling had been, whether it was intensive or not. If a single shell landed, people who were nearby would usually run to the place to help the wounded and then they would, themselves, take shelter until they could be sure that the shelling had stopped. If the shelling did not stop, they didn't leave their shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I was asking you about security.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, policemen were also wounded and killed in those places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But can you tell us how much time on the average elapsed from the time an incident took place to the time when security was put in place?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be precise about that. There were situations when it was not possible. It could be five minutes later or half an hour later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it sometimes happen that there would be shelling and you would receive information that the shell had not caused any damage or any casualties, and in that case would you not go to the spot at all?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not possible for a shell to land without causing any damage. It could happen that there were no casualties, but all shells that landed were recorded. It was always recorded at what time and place a shell had exploded and whether or not there had been injured persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But sometimes shell fragments, pieces of shrapnel would not be taken for analysis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever a team was established to carry out an onsite investigation, the traces had to be preserved and parts of the shell had to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But were there any cases of shelling where a team did not arrive on the spot where the shell had landed?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your previous statements in relation to the Markale II incident, as this was not within your competence, you said that in spite of this, you went there because somebody had told you, one of your superiors had told you to go and see if you could help. I may have misinterpreted your reply, but could you clarify this, please?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain once more how it came about that we went to help. At that time, we were having breakfast and we had actually just finished breakfast and were on our way to the police station. We heard the explosion. We did not know where it had taken place. When we got to the police station, the duty officer told us that a shell had exploded in front of the market and that there were many people who had been killed. He ordered that all available vehicles, we had two or three available at the time, that the drivers should go there to help transport the injured. And the rest of us who did not have vehicles also went down there so that we could offer assistance if it was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you arrived there, all the injured had already been taken away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, when I arrived in the vicinity near the cathedral from where you could see all this, some of the people who had been injured had been taken away, some who had been killed had not been taken away yet; they were still there. Our assistance was no longer required, and we returned to the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did a team arrive to carry out an onsite investigation? Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any team because I went back to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see representatives of UNPROFOR arriving?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that there was no official decision by the authorities of the Federation either of the city of Sarajevo or the state of the army prohibiting people gathering in public places?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible there may have been a decision prohibiting gatherings, but it would not have been possible to comply with it, because that part of the street, Mula Mustafe Baseskije Street, was the only street people could take and the only place where they could buy something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was not my question. In your statement which is part of the record here --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] and, Your Honours, that's Exhibit 51937.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said the police in Sarajevo banned people from gathering in public places, that's what it says in your statement. I'm asking you whether there was such a decision in place because that's what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1937. It's the statement made on the 22nd of November, 1995. It's part of the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see on the screen the statement in question. This is on page 3 of the B/C/S version, and I'm asking you only this, the fact that I read in your statement the sentence starts with the following words: "Since the police in Sarajevo placed a ban on public gathering," this is what it says in your statement which remains unchanged. And I'm asking you whether there was a ban, a police ban on public assembly? That's the only thing I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to reference a paragraph, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] paragraph 15, first sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it says here that the police in Sarajevo had forbidden the people in Sarajevo together in public places, I can't remember whether there was an official decision of the authorities to issue such a ban. However, from our superior officers, we received a task to warn people to leave such places as quickly as possible and not to expose themselves to any further danger from shelling. However, in those parts, it was very difficult to implement because those were the only places where they could buy food. One street that was protected from views they thought and I thought as well that I was safe, that I would not be injured or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because the buildings around are high-rise buildings, wouldn't that be the primary reason why you felt that way?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buildings were not high-rise buildings there. They were two or three storeys high. They -- this is the old part of the town. However, it was well protected from views.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the old part of the city, did you know where the BiH Army facilities were?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no army facilities in the old part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the BiH Army used civilian facilities as their locations?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never heard that members of the BiH Army were billeted in schools and kindergartens?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that part there are neither kindergartens or nursery schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you did hear that members of the BiH army were billeted in such buildings?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the municipality known as Stari Grad, the old city, and the only two kindergartens in the territory of our municipalities had been torched or burned from shelling at the very beginning of the war. One of such kindergartens was in the vicinity of council house or a town hall, and it was completely destroyed so that it could not serve any purpose. And there was another very small kindergarten in the street called Logadinor [phoen], at least that's what it was called at that time. And it could not accommodate more than ten children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of the BiH Army also used shops and stores as their locations?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stores and shops were impossible to use for that purpose. Those were very small rooms, especially in Stari Grad municipality where all the houses are really tiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in answering my learned friend's question, you said, and this is how I understood it, when you were serving in the JNA, you completed training to become a platoon commander, did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the school for reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the centre for training of state border patrol units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you never attended a school for reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the military as a foot soldier, then I served as a member of the artillery crew. That was the way it was done. I worked on the 72-millimetre mortar. I became private 1st class after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what you told us.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not officially the school for reserve officers. The schools for reserve officers in the JNA were well defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you didn't receive the rank of sergeant in the military?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I became corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the 122-millimetre mortar range is?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you joined the police in 1992, you were a technician and head of shift in Hydrogradina?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Hydrogradina. Yes, Hydrogradina was the name of the company where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you never came in touch with any weaponry when you were working at Hydrogradina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the Court please produce a document, because I intend to put to the witness some questions about the incident that took place in December. P415. In B/C/S I'm looking for page 5, and in English I believe it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. This was shown to you yesterday. As a member of this team you were assigned together with another colleague of yours to constitute a team on behalf of the police station Stari Grad; is that correct? You can find that under numbers 9 and 10?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce page -- the following page in both versions of the document. The following page in English as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we can see in this document that about 11 citizens provided statements, but you did not participate in taking the statements from any of these citizens that spoke about this incident.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether UNPROFOR members were in that place when the onsite inspection was carried out?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were not authorised to provide any estimates about the type of ammunition that was found on the spot, that was not within your purview, was it?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were not a ballistics expert, and you did not have any experience with ballistics expertise?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were not authorised, nor did you ever provide any estimates with regard to the direction and the type of projectiles involved in any of the incidents?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the official notes that we drafted, we could only mention that the projectile had arrived from this or that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to read back to you part of your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not part of the 92 ter package. This is on page 3729 of that transcript of Mr. Dozo 's testimony in that case. I have downloaded this from the court database.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the end of your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case, Judge Harhoff put some questions to you with regard to what you did during that December incident?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember some explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question was as follows, and it is on page 3729, line 8: [In English] "Were you authorised to make determination as to the type and practice and use in the shell incidents?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- we don't have the benefit of that copy, I'm not quite sure you are being quoted correctly on the transcript. Are you able to give us copies of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have single hard copy, Your Honours. I'm going to read again: "Well, were you authorised to make determination as to the type of projectile used in shell incident?" Your answer? Do remember your answer? Do you remember having answered that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what you are reading, then I suppose I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then on the same page, 3729, line 13: "The direction of fire was established by the expert who was a member of the investigation team. It wasn't my role to do so. My task was to assist them, or rather, to carry out orders given by investigating judge. When pieces of shell were found, we were to be -- we were to secure the area around the spot where the incident took place." [Interpretation] You said this under oath, do you remember? Do you still adhere by what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now page 3731, line 1, a question put to you by Mr. Tapuskovic and Milosevic's counsel: "During the investigation is it true that you were not sure whether the shell was fired from a gun, or was it any other type of gun?" [Interpretation] Your answer: [In English] "I did not conduct this investigation. It was done by the investigating judge. I was neither authorised, nor did I have experience to qualify or to categorized the type of the shell. I didn't know what kind of shell was involved." [Interpretation] Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You adhere by that today?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for the witness, thank you very much, Mr. Dozo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Any re-examination, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Briefly Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'd like to focus down on the site involving Dervisa Selmanovic, you were asked quite a bit of questioning yesterday and as well as the beginning of this morning in relation to the sniping incident that took place there. In yesterday's transcript you'd indicated that "the times were dangerous, it was dangerous to live there." And you were referring to Zaima Sarca Street, I believe is the pronunciation of that. Can you please describe for the Court what was the reality for the civilians who were living in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, it was impossible to live there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this question does not arise from my cross-examination. If the witness mentioned anything, this was still not within the context of my cross-examination, and the witness is now trying to testify about things that do not arise from my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Frankly, Your Honour, it's at page 4551, line 21, which is precisely within the cross-examination of Defence counsel from yesterday's transcript, so I'd ask to explore this further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have no access to page 4551. Let's see if we can get it. I am afraid my pages are still numbered 1 to 96.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I actually have page 90, line 2, from yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe Ms. Carter could read the question back to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm happy to do so. The question, it was in the context of asking this witness why he was not interviewing all the witnesses that saw this sniping take place, and the question starting at line 19 was: "Did you try in the meantime to go and look up her neighbours and ask for their opinion and information?" "A. They did not reside there, not all of them resided there at the time. The times were dangerous. It was dangerous to live there. "So you didn't go to Sedrenik once again to check on her? "The uniform police were in charge of that, and we go on from there." Sorry, I apparently speak very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So, yeah, if I understand you, you are following up the statement that the times were dangerous; it was dangerous to live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you still standing by your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please describe for the Court what was the reality for the civilians that lived in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain, and I can share with you what happened when we went to the site of an incident where there had been shooting. We had to enter the house through a window, climbing a ladder, because sniping fired from Spicasta Stijena was such that it was impossible to enter some of the houses in the normal way, through the door. People normally came back to their houses in the evening, in the evening hours, and they would leave them very early in the morning while it was still dark. The then civilian protection would patrol the exposed areas during the night, and they would try and protect the areas exposed to sniping fire by extending wire and placing bed sheets or blankets, hanging those from the wires in order to block the line of sight to the snipers that were on Spicasta Stijena. A lot of the population of Sedrenik had moved out to the safer parts of the town. Every time we had to carry out an onsite inspection in Sedrenik, we were exposed to a great danger, and there was an imminent risk that we would not come back alive from such expeditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Defence counsel yesterday also questioned you in regards to the investigations that took place in that area. And you indicated at the time that you could not give another specific name to a sniping incident. But in your answer that you just gave, you seem to imply that there were a number of investigates performed, can you please estimate for the court how many investigations were performed in that area.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but there were a lot. Sniping, fire and shelling happened every day. There was no single day when somebody was not hurt or killed in Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now you are talking about that daily activity, and we see in P1940, and that's the statement of Ms. Selmanovic, that she said that not only did the bullet that hit her get fired that day, but there's also another 20 to 30. You indicated yesterday on top of that when you arrived several days later to perform the onsite investigation, you were coming under fire yet again and taking shelter behind a house. When you are talking about sniping, are you talking about a single bullet fired at a single person or something more aggressive?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It rarely happened that one single bullet was fired from Spicasta Stijena. Very often, if not all the time, sniping activity involved a person firing from Spicasta Stijena on anything that he could see moving about.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who controlled Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment when the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina started, the Spicasta Stijena was under the control of the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Were there any other lines of sight or lines of fire into Sedrenik outside of Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sniping activity against Sedrenik could come only from Spicasta Stijena, whereas shells could have come from all parts of town which were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Why do you say that the only area that sniping could come from was Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIB DOZO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spicasta Stijena is the only elevation above Sedrenik, on the left was Grdonj, and behind Grdonj were the lines of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. From that side you could neither approach or see Sedrenik. And the right-hand side is a forest called Alipashino Brdo. And from there, Sedrenik is not visible. There is no clear line of vision from there towards Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I thank you for your time as well as your testimony. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter. Thank you, very much, Mr. Dozo, that brings us to the end of your testimony. We thank you for coming to testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down, and will you please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time Ms. Bolton will be taking the next witness, and I would asked to be excused from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused, Madam Carter. Madam Bolton. Would it be an appropriate time, Madam Bolton, or would you want to start?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I would actually like to perhaps move up where Ms. Carter is. So if we could take the recess now that would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Bolton, you can explain the protective measures to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, for the record, there are protective measure that is were granted in a previous proceeding and are continued therefore under Rule 75, and that consists of image distortion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm just having a bit of trouble hearing Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have a problem hearing me?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I was, but that seem to have corrected it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljic, you speak both B/C/S and fairly good English; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I will just remind you then, that notwithstanding the fact that you may understand or think you understand my question in English, it's important that you wait for the translation. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just indicate to the court what your educational background is.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: During the war, if that's what you are asking me, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking about your formal education.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I have a degree in engineering.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What kind of engineering?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I have a degree from the Sarajevo University in 1991 in October, and the degree I obtained was in General engineering.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did your studies include any studies in the law of physics, and the laws of physics?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Of course, those were compulsory subjects in my junior year, physics, mathematics.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were you residing in Sarajevo when the hostilities broke out?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you continue to reside in Sarajevo after the hostilities broke out?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I continued to reside there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when the hostilities first broke out, at that time was the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina an organised army in existence at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: At first when the conflict broke out, it was the so-called Territorial Defence, the army was established only later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you participate in the Territorial Defence at all?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I did. I was a member of the Territorial Defence, which bore the name of our local commune fraternity and unit in new Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How many months or years were you part of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: From April or the end of April 1992, to July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what happened in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: In July 1993, I joined the Ministry of the Interior as a member of the security services centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was your position?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: My position was an expert for mechanical traces and ballistics at the security services centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And prior to taking up that position, had you had any experience in ballistics?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you receive any training?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: As soon as I joined the police, I had a nine-and-a-half-month training. My mentors were my senior colleagues who had already worked as ballistics experts and experts for mechanical tracers in the same ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who were those senior colleagues primarily?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The late Borislav Stankov, the late Zlatko Medjedovic, and the late Hamdija Cavcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you are using the term "late," take it you mean that they are all now deceased?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes. Unfortunately, they died after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the training that you received, then, you indicated you had so the mentors, was there any element that was more traditional method, like reading of books or study materials?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I can say that the training was a bit out of the ordinary and faced with the unfortunate circumstances, I had the good fortune of learning much faster than one would under normal circumstances. It was already wartime, and I just had to acquire knowledge much faster.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you are talking about mentoring, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: That means that my senior colleagues were also my trainers and my mentors, and I had to take my final exam before them as members of a commission which consisted of several other people as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you pass that, I don't know if it was oral or written, examination?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It consisted of two parts, one was oral another was written, of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you have occasion during the war, then, to be involved in any investigations relating to sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I want to ask you if you had any involvement in investigations where trams were hit by sniper bullets?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Court, first, when you got a call to, I take it, participate in an investigation of a tram sniping incident, what was the purpose of the investigation? What were you trying to ascertain?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Our team consisted of several people, and the role of a ballistics expert in the team was to ascertain the direction from which the bullet came and the type of the projectile. And that was the main task of the ballistics expert on any team if this is what you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. Could you walk us through the methodology that you would follow then from the moment, I guess, you would arrive on site to investigate a tram incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Usually we insisted on the tram remaining in the place where the incident happened. However, due to the circumstances that was often impossible. However, our part of the job was, as I've already told you, to ascertain the direction from which the bullet or bullets came, and to try and ascertain the type of the projectile. And the rest of the team worked on collecting evidence and marking the traces on the spot and the consequences that were due to the action of one or several projectiles. The whole work was led by an investigative judge because without his order, our team and our colleagues from the crime prevention police would not have been able to access the scene of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You've told us that the purpose was to try -- or one of the purposes was to try to ascertain the direction from which the bullet or bullets came. So what evidence would you look at to assist you in making that determination?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The main thing was to determine the positions of the damage on the tram or car or vehicle, to identify entry holes and possibly exit holes, and try to establish using simple methods, the direction from which the shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Is there a method you used, or how would you distinguish what was an entry hole or an exit hole through a tram?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: In many books, and in the ballistics literature about the traces left by fire-arms, it's easy to determine what entry and exit holes look like. You look at the traces on the materiel. You look at the direction in which fibres are bent and so on. And to determine the angle, we used a very simple method using a metal cube, a small metal cube or rod, and a rope. This was part of the equipment carried by forensic technicians, and we would then link up the entry and exit holes, thus determining from where the bullet had come because we wanted to establish the direction from which the projectile had come, and also the type of projectile or bullet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Just continuing or picking up on what you are saying about determining the direction then, you are talking about using this pole and rope, I take it, to connect the entrance and the exit holes, how does that then extrapolate into knowing the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: We used that to establish the angle of entry. This is classical geometry. You push a tube through the entry hole, you stretch the string to the place where the bullet ended its trajectory, the exit hole, and theoretically, you can extend this using an optical device to infinity. And then that makes it possible to determine the area from which the bullet arrived. You use mathematical methods to calculate the angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you say you use an optical device to stretch possibly to infinity, which direction would you be pointing your optical device relative to the entrance hole?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, of course in the direction of the entry hole, you would look from the inside towards the outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. When you talked about looking at the damage to the tram, you indicated that you would look for entry holes, and you said possibly exit holes. Can you explain why there wouldn't be necessarily an exit hole?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Sometimes a bullet would stay. If you are asking me about the tram, it would get stuck. It would get stuck against a metal sheet. It couldn't pierce, for example, and then we would not be able to find an exit hole.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. You indicated it would be preferable when you did these investigations if the tram were still in the place where it had been struck, you said that wasn't always possible. Why wasn't it always possible?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Because of the precision with which the place from which the shot was fired had to be established. It would have been a good thing for the vehicle to return to the place where it had been hit. However, in most cases because the tram driver was in a panic, or because the shooting went on, or because of other circumstances, the tram would continue driving, and we would probably arrive -- most often we would arrive on the scene once the shooting had already stopped, in order to avoid unnecessary casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, in cases where the tram had been moved then, was it possible for you to take into consideration the movement of the tram when you were trying to ascertain the origin or direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: By the kind of traces on the tram, and the statements made by the people involved in the event, we were able to establish the direction, but never the precise spot from which the bullet had been fired. So we would say it had come from the general area of so and so. Since the vehicle had already moved, we could not pin-point the precise feature. We could only say that the bullet had come from the south-east or the south-west, or it would all depend on the position of the tram. You could say it had come from above or from left to right and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how generally would you know if the tram had been located -- sorry, had been moved subsequent to the firing? How would you know where it had been at the time of the firing?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Based on the statements given by the tram driver and the evidence collected by our colleagues in the crime investigation police. Also from the passengers in the tram, those who had been wounded, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I wonder, Madam Registrar, if we could please bring up 65 ter 8600. And, Madam Usher, the witness is going to need to use the magic pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: First, I should ask if you recognise the area depicted in the photograph before you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, it's parts of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And is the tram line visible on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just using your finger, can you point out where the tram line runs. Sorry, I guess you have to use the pen to show where the tram line runs.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: And so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what is the name of that street that it runs on?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Now it's called Zmaja od Bosne. It used to be called Vojvode Putnika and in the opposite direction coming from town, it's called Marsala Tita.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in terms of geography, is this line -- does this run basically east west, north south, some other direction?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: East west.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you assist me in identifying some of the buildings in is this photo, please. First, do you see the Marshal Tito barracks? Sorry, I didn't get a translation of whatever you just said?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The street?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, the barracks buildings for the Marshal Tito?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: These, this is the barracks, this whole compound here. That's the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you write the initials MTB on what you've circled?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: B as in --

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: MTB.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you see the school of technology on this photograph? If so, could you mark it with the initial T?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. How about the museum of the revolution; is that visible? Could you circle it, if it is.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, it's visible. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you put an M there, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is there something called the earth museum visible?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you put an E there, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is a street made reference to at some parts of this case called, and I apologise in advance for the pronunciation, Lenjinova Street. Do you know what Street I'm talking about? Is that visible?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: In part here in front of these sky scrapers here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And are you familiar with a building called the Metalka building? If so, could you circle it. Could you write the initials MET.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I wonder if this could please be tendered as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1944, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could just leave it on the screen for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There are four high-rise buildings on the far left side of the screen right by where you've indicated Lenjinova Street is. In what area or part of town are those four high-rises situate?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how about the Metalka building, what part of town is it situated in?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: That's Grbavica to, the beginning of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And during the conflict, which army controlled Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn, now, sir -- I'm going to be asking you about two specific investigations into tram sniping incidents. And for the record, to assist the Court, the first one we have on the indictment as B8. It's an incident from the 23rd of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we have, please, 65 ter 08612. And if the witness can also be shown page 2 of the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: That is a report drawn up by my colleagues from the crime police, Dragan Miokovic and Kemal Buco.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity during your proofing session earlier this week to review this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, you showed it to me; I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did it accurately reflect your investigation and your findings?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could go back to page 1, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at the first page, we see both your name, sir, and the name of Zlatko Medjedovic, was that one of the gentlemen you mentioned earlier as one of your mentors?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, we usually went out as a team, Zlatko or Boro or Hamdija, and I, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in terms of the direction of the tram in relation -- that it was travelling regards to this incidents, sir, which direction was it travelling?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It was travelling from the centre towards the new part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Would that be eastbound or westbound, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: From the east towards the west, so westbound.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was your understanding in relation to this incident in terms of where the tram had been situated at the time the sniping began?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: According to our information, it was between the technical school and the Marshal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to, I guess, a blank copy of 65 ter 8600.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, I suppose you are still coming back to this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I will be coming back to it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you just assist us in terms of - I'm sorry, Madam Usher, I'll need your assistance again - perhaps drawing a circle around the area that is denoted as being between the technical school and the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: This entire area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand. Is that entire area between the barracks and the technical school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and that was the route the tram was taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but the question was no to show the route that the tram was taking but to circle the area that is between the barracks and the technical school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was your question, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just so we are clear, sir, can you remind us again of where the technical school was.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: This is the technical school.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you put a T in that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you remind us again of where the barracks extend to and from.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The barracks extends from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So the area you first circled seems to extend from the far east side of the technical school to the most westernly point on the Marshal Tito barracks, then when his honour posed the question again, you circled the smaller area. And I don't understand what the smaller area is supposed to indicate.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The smaller circle is the precise area in between the technical school and the Marshal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, do you understand what the bigger area is supposed to signify?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Maybe I can rephrase the question, sir. Does one of those two areas that you've drawn on the map, does that designate where you understood the tram had been located at the time it was hit by the sniper bullets?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: According to eye-witness statements, and the statement of the driver, he said the tram was somewhere in the bigger circle that I first made.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So I want to be able to mark this so that it's understandable later. The bigger circle then, sir, if you could -- could you write the word "tram" on the bigger circle.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in the box you drew above to show the Marshal Tito barracks, again could you mark it with MTB?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Are the -- within this photo, how many tram stops, if any, are actually visible?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you mark where those stops are located, please. Could you use the numbers 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Number 1 is near the technical school. And number 2 is at the Marshal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We've heard some evidence in these proceedings about a stop called Marindvor. Where is it relative to this photo, if it's not visible?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It's on this side here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you put a 3 there.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have a 2 anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: 2 is way over on the left side of the photo, Your Honour, on top of the building. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I think we are done with the pen for now, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In this -- if we could go back to 65 ter 8th 08612, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, what do you want to do with this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I do wish to tender this as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1945, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I don't seem to remember admitting the first 8600.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's already an Exhibit P100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it? No, no, the one marked by this witness earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That was Exhibit P1944, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we can scroll down in both versions, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what, if any, damage you found to the tram on examination that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. You can find it in the report. We managed to detect that in the first case it was just one bullet of an unknown calibre that burst, leaving two bullet traces on the tram.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say the bullet burst?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Due to the impact against a hard surface, the bullet shattered, fragmented, thus we could not find the whole of the bullet. We only found fragments thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And what hard surface did it hit that caused it to fragment?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It was a metal plate in the tram, and as a result it fragmented.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Where was that metal plate in the tram?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: In this case it was inside the tram on the wall, on the interior tram wall where the bullet hit. To be more precise, it was in the upper right-hand side corner of the tram's window frame. You will find that in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And which side of the tram would have been hit if this tram -- we've already indicated was travelling westbound, would it be the north or the south side of the tram where the damage was found?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: As the tram was moving from the east to the west, if you are looking from the driver's position, it came from the left-hand side of the tram.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you are looking from the driver's position facing in the direction in which you are travelling or facing the back of the tram?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: As the tram moves, in the direction of the tram's movement, the bullet came from its left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And were you able to make a determination in this case as to the likely origin of the bullet that hit tram 263?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: In this particular case, it was not possible to determine the facility, but we were able to ascertain that it came from the Sector South, from the area of Grbavica. We were not able to determine the exact place, and I have already explained why. The tram had been moved from the place where it was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And just so the record is clear, if we could turn to the second page of the B/C/S version of this report and the English version of this report, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The tram we were just talking about was tram 263. And this page of the report, sir, what tram number does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Tram number 238.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So there were actually two separate incidents that were investigated and discussed in this report; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, because they took place in the course of the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I wonder if that could be marked as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1946, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, to a second incident, which for the record is scheduled incident B10 in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 3412 up, please. I should indicate, Your Honours, that the B/C/S version of Exhibit -- or of 65 ter 3412 includes all the pages, and the English translations are actually found at different parts in 65 ter 3412.01 through .15 or .115, and I'll be referring to the different 65 ter numbers as need be to correspond to the English versions.
