utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could return your attention, sir, to the actual B/C/S exhibit, can you tell us if you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 in the B/C/S version, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is this a matter that you participated in the onsite investigation in relation to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. My name is also here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity during our proofing session earlier in the week to review the entire B/C/S version of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I've had an occasion to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Does the report accord with your recollection of the actual investigation and your findings?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you tell us in relation to this incident, sir, and let us know if you need to refresh your memory from the report, which direction you understood this tram was travelling at the time it was struck?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: This tram was moving from the direction of centre into the direction of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And would that be then eastbound or westbound?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: From east to west. Westbound.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And again can you tell us where you understood this tram was located at the time that it was struck by the sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It just started moving from the tram station in front of the Marshal Tito barracks in the direction of new Sarajevo, and that's the moment when it was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could again bring up a blank version of 65 ter 8600, please. Sorry. Again, Madam Usher, if I could have your assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you again just circle for us the area where you understood the tram was located in relation to this incident when it was struck?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: This is the place, the tram stop known as the Marshal Tito barracks stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Where is the -- is there a tram stop called the KMT tram stop? Is that the same thing or something different?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It's one in the same. There's no other.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where did you receive your information about the location of the tram in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The key factor was the statement provided by the tram driver, but there were also other eye-witnesses, you can find that in the official note.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to this tram, were you able to make --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could tender that as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't want to tell us what that circle is called? You've been giving them names like MTB.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Certainly, could you mark that, sir, as -- I want to call it the tram stop. Are you able to write tram stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1947, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could return - thank you, Madam Usher - to 65 ter 3412. And I'd like to go to page 4 of that document, Madam Registrar. I understand that actually the exhibits, the English copy is not in separate exhibits. So in the English version if you could go back one page, please. Sorry, could you go forward two pages. Forward one more page, please, in the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In relation to this investigation, sir, were you able to make any determination as to the likely origin or source of the sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, we managed to do that. There were several places where the tram was damaged, so we determined that the projectile came from the direction of Grbavica, the south-east direction in relation to the way the tram was moving.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in relation to this incident, were you able to be any more precise than saying that it had simply come from Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: In that particular case, we were able to determine that fire was open from the Grbavica sector, and to be more precise, from the direction of the high-rise building in the Novaljeva [phoen] street.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that conclusion would have been based simply on the results of the ballistic examination or testimony from -- or statements from witnesses or both?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Both sources were relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when we are talking about those buildings, if we could go back to the last photograph we marked, which I think was Exhibit, I think, P46 -- 1946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this, just to refresh my memory, this is the incident in which the bullet is supposed to have disintegrated?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think you are think being another incident, I'm not sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just to answer His Honour's question, sir, in relation to this incident, if you recall, how many bullet marks were there found in the tram?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you recall if all eight bullets were recovered from inside the tram?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Only two because the others were stuck between the outer wall and the inner wall of the tram's carriage.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Only two, what do you mean by only two were what?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Two bullets had an entry and exit holes in the tram, which means they pierced through both of the tram carriage walls and injured some of the passengers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Before we get back to the photo, can you just explain, is it possible for one bullet to injure more than one person?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: In this particular case, given the short distance and high energy that a bullet has, there were a lot of people in the tram, it was crowded, the bullet will find it easy to pass through all the soft tissues on its way until it hits the first firmer and stronger surface, harder surface. So it is possible that one bullet inflicted wounds on two or more people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. When we are talking looking at the photograph that is back in front of you about the high-rise buildings on Lenjinova Street, how would the numbering go if we are indicating that the likely source of fire was the fourth high-rise building, which one would be the fourth?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll use number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, we have the photo on screen, I'm not sure if you can see on this photo a location called the Vrbanja bridge. Is that visible on this photo?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Vrbanja. This is the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you put a V there, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And would it be possible, sir, for bullets fired from the Vrbanja bridge to reach the location of this tram at the time of the sniping incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Impossible, there are so many obstacles to the tram stop, and the tram stop is not visible from that place anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If a snap-shot could be taken of that photograph, please, Your Honour, and be marked as an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1948, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Brief indulgence, please. Just with respect to the report, Your Honour, I don't think there's any need to go back to at this point. This would be 65 ter 3412. Could it be marked as an exhibit as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1949, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You had indicated in relation to this last incident we were discussing, sir, that your service had determined that the likely source of fire was that fourth high-rise building on Lenjinova Street in Grbavica. Did you ever have occasion after the hostilities had ceased to go to any of those high-rise buildings on that street?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When was that done?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: After the Dayton Accords, and the reintegration of Grbavica, which was in February and March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And were you there in a personal capacity or professional capacity?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It was on the order of the investigating judge for professional reasons and also an order of the chief of the crime prevention police to check out all those facilities for which there was reasonable grounds to suspect that they served as firing positions during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you -- did you visit each of those four buildings?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. Each of the four, but not every apartment. And also we inspected the Metalka building.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you are talking about we, who else was with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatko Medjedovic, Mr. Borislav Stankov, a member of the crime police, a judge, and members of the police station Novo Sarajevo given the fact that Grbavica falls under the jurisdiction of that police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Bolton, in the answer to the previous question, you said you said each of the four but not every apartment, and also you inspected the what building?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I believe he said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Metalka building also in Grbavica. Metalka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you been shown the Metalka building in any the be exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, he marked it on the very first map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So dealing first then with the four high-rise buildings we were discussing, sir, can you tell us when you went into those buildings, what did you locate?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: At the higher floors of the buildings for which it could be assumed that they served as firing positions during the war, we found five or six apartments which had been redesigned to serve as sniper nests.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you describe what each of these -- firstly did the apartments all look similar, or were they different setups?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: All of these looked the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was the general setup then?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The general setup was as follows: Petition walls that divided the rooms were partly pierced. The outer wall facing the streets of Zmaja od Bosne and Marshal Tito, or rather the side across the Miljacka river which was under the control of the BiH Army had a small opening. And within each of the apartments, partition walls had been demolished and openings had been made which were conical in shape so that the sharp-shooter could fire from within the apartment in the depth of the apartment where the opening was small. He would have a clear vision of the enemy, and the enemy would have a very difficult time spotting the sharp-shooter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How many walls then would have separated the sniper from fire coming into the building?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Are you referring to the perforated walls? If that's the case, at least three, so that sniper shooter would be opening fire from the third room in a row, behind the third wall in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to look out through those openings that you've described towards the tram tracks?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Of course, yes, it was a unique opportunity. I had never seen anything of the kind before that. My senior colleagues Zlatko and Boro actually provided explanation as to what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. When you looked out from the position you believe the sniper had taken, how much of the tram tracks could you see?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I could see the complete stretch from the Holiday Inn to the school of science and mathematics, i.e., the high-rise that blocks the view after that. And you could have that view from of the four high-rise buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at the map that's still on the screen, is the school of mathematics visible?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Where would it be relative to what is visible?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It would be to the west of the barracks in the direction of Novi Grad, the new part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I can draw an arrow on the photo if you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you do that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: So it would be in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you just write "math", m-a-t-h.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, and could you circle for us the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if you could just write an HI.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Were there any -- sorry, how many storeys up in these buildings on average were these six apartments?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: You mean how many floors did these high-rise buildings have? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicated that you had found -- you had hadn't examined every apartment, but you had located approximately six apartments where you had these -- which you believe to have been used by snipers. I'm just wondering how many storeys up in the buildings those apartments were located.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: They were all higher than ten floors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were they on different floors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At this point in time is it possible for you remember exactly what floor on which building the apartments were located?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's very difficult, they were all higher than the 10th floor, but for me to say precisely, probably there is documentation in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I just want you to mark one last thing on this diagram and that is just to refresh the Court's memory as to which building is the Metalka building. Could you again circle the Metalka building and write MET.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Metalka, MET.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher. That's everything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you indicated earlier that you had the opportunity also to perform a post-war inspection of this building?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you find any apartments within that building that appeared to have been used by snipers?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: We didn't find that sort of shelter here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Again, were you able to go into every apartment in that building?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Not each and every one. Only some that we suspected might have been used. The ones on the highest floors in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If a snap could be made of that, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It would be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back a quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm counsel Novak Lukic and on behalf of Mr. Perisic and his Defence team, I will putting questions to you. You have testified before this Tribunal on two occasions and you know that when we speak the same language, there is a problem with interpretation. The interpretation has to be on the record, so please, we must both try to make a pause between question and answer so that everything gets interpreted. I'll put a few questions to you about a topic broached by Madam Bolton which has do with your career. And most especially in the period when you were a member of the BH Army, as I'll be calling it. I understood you to say in the course of your testimony, that in April 1992 you were in the Territorial Defence. We know that in the late spring and early summer of 1992, the army of BH began to be formed, partly from the structures of the Territorial Defence. When did you actually become a member of the BH Army, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I entered the Territorial Defence toward the end of April 1992. And when the army was established around June, our unit, which was called the brotherhood and Unity Territorial Defence became part of the Motarised Brigade. That was around June 1992 when the army came into existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you remained there until the summer of 1993 when you transferred to the police?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this period, while you were a member of the BH Army, I read in your statements that you were mostly at Hrasno Brdo, and Stup, at those positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes. When the conflict first broke out, we assisted the police forces in the area of the school of mechanical engineering, Elektroprivreda, and then they sent us to Hrasno Brdo. And later on when the motorised unit was established, our area of responsibility was Stup. And that's where I was last with the army before I transferred to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I also think I found in your statements that while serving in the army, you would spend a week at the positions and then a week at home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: In the beginning until we went to Stup, as I lived nearby, and near the school of economics, we would spend one night on guard duty and we would have one night off. However, when I went to Stup, which was quite far away from my home, and the units became larger, we were required to spend seven days at the positions, and then we would be off for seven days, and we could go home if we could, so what you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware whether the same situation obtained elsewhere in the Defence of Sarajevo? In other words, there were no situations where the soldiers would be in a barracks far away from their homes?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't want to prejudge this issue because I don't really no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have on the screen 65 ter document 9244. It's a map and I see that you testified about this at the previous trial, and I would like this Chamber also to get an idea of this. So let's look at the map of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the map to come up, sir, do you agree with me that during the war from 1992 until the Dayton Accords in the Sarajevo war theatre, the units and forces holding certain positions didn't shift much, they were rather static?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please, I need your assistance. [Interpretation] Could we zoom in a little bit, please. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, now, you said that you were aware that the BH Army held positions on the hill of Zuc. Could you please mark the hill of Zuc with a number 1. We can move through this part very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Here it is. I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you find Stup, the part where you were, the hill and village of Stup, or the neighbourhood of Stup, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Around here, more or less. In the direction of Vlasici, the Hladnjaca, that's the area our unit held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you mark it with a 2.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The neighbourhood of Mojmilo and Mojmilo hill was also a position held by the BH Army. Could you mark that location approximately on this map, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: With a number 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I think this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mount Igman, you can mark it with a number 4 and indicate the direction.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Here it is overlooking Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And those were also positions held by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this map --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's take a larger map. Can this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours, and then can we have a blank map -- a copy of the map brought up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in, into the centre of the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the location of Debelo Brdo here, more or less, with a number 1.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this location was also held by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In front of this location towards the centre is the Jewish cemetery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the Jewish cemetery, please, with a number 2.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I'll do my best. I think this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this location was held in part by the BH Army and in part by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I agree, it was more or less no-man's lands, I mean the cemetery itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And looking towards the centre of town, it leads towards the Holiday Inn and the Zmaja od Bosne Street?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, standing at the Jewish cemetery and looking strait ahead, it comes out on the Marindvor, that street. You can see all of if from the Jewish cemetery. I didn't really have occasion to view it from up there, but I assume that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are aware that on Grdonj hill, there was also a position of the BH Army, could you mark that with a 3, please, and Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, Grdonj hill near Sedrenik. It looks down on Sedrenik on one side on Rijeka on the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. Just with respect to that last marking, and it happened once on the previous map, my friend indicated that a position was held by the BH Army and asked him to mark it without asking the witness if he agreed that it was held bit BH Army. I think he corrected it with respect to the last map. But with respect to the number 3 here, I think he should be putting to the witness before he has him mark it on the map whether he agrees it was in fact held by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I did ask the witness that. It may be a discrepancy in interpretation, but I think the witness agreed that all the positions I asked him about so far were held by the BH Army, both on the previous map and on this one. Now I asked specifically about the Jewish cemetery, asking whether this was the border-line belt of both armies. I think that is how the witness understood my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the record not absolutely clear, Mr. Lukic. If you can just find out from the witness. Sir, was Grdonj hill held by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the record is clear. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on this map do you see Colina Kapa, and do you know who held that position? If you do see it, please mark it with a number 4.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I do see Colina Kapa. I'm marking it with a 4. It was the observatory, and it was held by the VRS. It was a prominent elevation, whereas the lower Colina Kapa was held by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Grbavica, I won't ask you to mark it on this map, but you said it was controlled by the VRS. Do you agree with me that Grbavica was surrounded on three sides by positions of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that in the course of the war you didn't go there, but do you know that it was inhabited by civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: You mean Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And when the reintegration took place, some of them stayed behind and testified to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see Hrasnica on this map and tell us who held that position?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Hrasnica was held by the BH Army. Just a moment. But you can't see it here on this map. It's behind Butmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you just mark the direction with an arrow and mark it with a number 5.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this map also be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D70, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll go back now to the main topic of your testimony here. When you were doing your part of the ballistics work, you had two tasks to the best of my understanding, to give your opinion on the type of projectile that had caused a certain incident; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And to give your opinion as to the direction from which the projectile had arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you told Ms. Bolton a little while ago, I understood you to say that when you couldn't pin-point the precise location from which a projectile had come, you would say it came from the general area of, in order to be professional and correct in your opinion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your part of the ballistics report, which was probably included in a more comprehensive report, you never used the term from the direction of the aggressor's position, because you couldn't actually determine that with precision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: We used the term from the area under the control of such and such an army, based on objective findings, but we did not use the term "aggressor" in our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But in your reports, besides the direction, you -- you could tell the direction, but you couldn't tell the distance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: No, we did not establish the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if in a certain direction there were positions, both of the BH Army and the VRS, your conclusion that a projectile had arrived from the territory of the VRS was based on witness statements, but not on materiel traces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: We would mention an area under the control of such and such an army, only if we were sure there were no positions of the other army nearby. Otherwise, we would just say that the projectile had come from the north, south, east, or west, and so on. So we always made sure that we avoided mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if there were two opposing armies there, you did not establish anything else apart from the direction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said, and I have to check this with you, when asked by Ms. Bolton today, you said that after completing your training, your specialist training in ballistics, you passed an exam. That's what you said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read out to you part of the record of your testimony in the Galic case. The date is the 11th of March, 2002. Page 5118, line 10: "Q. Now, did you take any examinations in respect of your training as a ballistic analyst? [Interpretation] Your answer: "A. No."

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: The question was probably whether before I joined the police I had taken any exams during my university studies having do with ballistics. And that is correct, I did not. I only passed the test after my training. I had to get a certificate in order to be able to sign my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've clarified that point. Did you find yourself in a situation or hear that members of UNPROFOR who were there to conduct onsite investigations at the same time as you, that they were prevented by the military authorities from attending at an onsite investigation.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I've heard of such a thing happening. We insisted, we from the police, from the technical service, we insisted that UNPROFOR be there and as to their being prevented, this is the first I've heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that after the fragments were taken for analysis, after they arrived in your laboratories or your institutions, UNPROFOR asked to be given access to these fragments?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, but only in cases of more serious shelling. However, as regards sniping, nobody ever came to inquire about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Another general question. Do you share my opinion that the media, especially the Serbian media, expressed the viewpoint that certain incidents had been staged by the authorities of the Muslim Federation. Do you remember such stories going around?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not sure that I appreciate the relevance of a question that starts, Do you share my opinion about something that was reported by the Serbian media. I think he is asking the witness to express an opinion about what was expressed in the Serbian media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have formulated my question clumsily, and I'll reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that in certain media, sometimes certain incidents were represented as being staged?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this usually had to do with serious events, those that were high-profile events in the media?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Precisely so. THE COURT: Sorry, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, again I don't quite understand the relevance of this line of questioning with this witness. This seems to be just talking about having heard rumours about what the Serb position was. I don't know what time-frame we are talking about, if we are talking during the war, if we are talking after the war. I just don't see how the relevance of this line of questioning or the ability of this witness to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is highly relevant, and the OTP frequently when putting forward their evidence asked witnesses about the way events were represented in the media. And I am asking about specific issues here, about onsite investigations, and I certainly wish to put certain things to the witness that have to do with my case. I think it's highly relevant for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. Lukic, is that you are not asking him what he saw in the media and at what time. You are asking him if he did hear that in the media -- I'll cite you to the correct, to the specific question. That is page 65 line 15: "Did you hear that in certain media sometimes certain incidents were represented as being staged?" In fact, when Madam Bolton stood up, I was about to intervene and ask the witness, from whom did he hear, at what time in the history of the war did he hear, because -- I see you frowning, but your question says, Did you hear? In other words, he didn't see this misrepresentation in the media he only heard about it, from whom did he hear it, and when did he hear it? That's the nub of the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand, Your Honour. And the gestures I was making were those of approval and understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for explaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question, Witness, is the following: In relation to the Markale II incident which took place in August 1995, are you aware that it was represented in certain media as having been staged by members of the authorities of the BH Federation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, but I learned about that only after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to Markale I, an incident which took place in February 1994 that similar -- similar ideas were being put forward in the media?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I learned about that after the war too. There was some broadcasts on television about that. Not the Bosnian television, but the Serbian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to follow Serbian media during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: When there was electricity, I was keen to hear the other side as well, so I listened to the Crna radio programme, and I sometimes watched TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's just be very precise for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. When you say Crna, this is the news agency of Republika Srpska; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you something about the two incidents that you testified about. I have a couple of questions for you. The incident B8, which happened on the 23rd of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce P1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've had an occasion to see the document, and what I concluded from the testimonies in evidence before this court, and you tell me if I'm right or wrong, is that the entry damage from the outer wall side of the tram was not found, and based on that, it was concluded that the bullet must have entered through an open window.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, you will find it in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in the interior part of the tram, and I suppose on the opposite side from that window, two damaged areas were found, and based on that, you concluded that the bullet must have been fragmented.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No projectile particle was found on the spot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: No, you are not right. There were some particles which were found, a cartridge was found, I think. So we couldn't actually, based on the fragments that were found, we could not determine the type of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on the facts that you were seized with, pointing to just one bullet, could you conclude that the first point of impact was the interior wall of the tram or was -- and then hit the soft tissue of some persons in the tram? Or was it the other way around, did the bullet first go through the soft tissue of the passengers and then ended up on a hard surface?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: It first hit a hard surface. It was then fragmented, and the fragments injured the two persons on the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this thesis which was the basis of your conclusion, was it corroborated by the injuries sustained by the individuals who were wounded by the level of their entry and exit wounds?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: We did not take into account those persons injuries because both the tram and the persons had already been moved from the site of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a correction for in the transcript. Page 68, line 21, after my question is actually the witness's answer, which is not clearly indicated. Line 21 through line 23 where a new question starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any regular ballistics report about such a situation, one should take into account the measurements of the entry and exit wounds on the bodies of the injured persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances. However, it was very hard to implement in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The onsite investigation of this incident as far as I could tell was carried out in the tram garage, in the tram depot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We insisted on the tram being returned to the site of the incident. However, the investigating judge was the team leader, and he made the call.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And under such circumstances, you established the point of contact, i.e., the place where the tram was when it was hit based exclusively on the eye-witnesses' statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also in such situations since you did not have the exit point of the bullet, and you were not able to draw a straight line from there to the exit point, you could not establish the angle at which the bullet entered the tram apparently through an open window?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: You are right, we couldn't do that. We could not determine the angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court produce the photo under 65 ter 8600. Which is the photo that we have already looked at with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the photo again, and mark the Metalka building. Please place number 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Shall I put a circle around it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The building next to it on the right-hand side, do you know whose forces were there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Nobody's.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please make a circle around there and put number 2 next to it.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you testified in the Dragomir Milosevic case on page 4760, did you say about this building as follows: The question was actually as follows, line 8, page 4760: [In English] "Q. Can you tell me behind this building, this building were belonged to the BH Army?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "A. No, they were all under the control of VRS except for the front one that resembled Metalka, and half of that building was practically no-man's land. Both parties used to take position there, but those were not permanent positions, as much as I was able to gather with regard to the situation on the front."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you look at page 70, lines 21 to 23, and check whether they represent exactly what you read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall read this again. [In English] "Q. Can you tell me behind this building, this rectangle building" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton is on her feet. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. My concern is that the witness is being read a portion of a transcript without really being taken, I think, to the portion of the transcript that might give him an idea of the context. It's a question out of the blue. His testimony was quite lengthy in Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to clarify that in the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that's the practice in this court, then that's the practice I'll follow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the thing is I'm not sure whether -- or I am not aware of one counsel -- a practice where one counsel tells another how to ask questions. Now he is asking questions from what he sees, and if you think that because of the context he is misrepresenting the situation, it's for you when you re-examine to clarify the situation. Otherwise, I'm not -- I don't see with on what ground you are standing up, if you are objecting at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My objection would be based on the practice at home which is one where in fairness to the witness, if you think the context isn't clear, you would object in cross-examination. But the practice here seems to be that I would just correct it in re-examination, so I will absolutely follow this practice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not want to confuse the witness. I'm just trying to understand some things from the transcript. I've not now had an opportunity to look at the photo before, and I want to clarify things with the witness. I'm going to read the question again: [In English] "Q. Can you tell me behind this building, this rectangle building, were belonging to the BH Army?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Read what is being typed. Is that correct on the transcript here now? Here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is one word that's incorrect, Your Honour, and that is this as opposed to "these".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say it's supposed to be "these."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "These," yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the word following after that that says building is still in the singular?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Rectangle building, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the building before this rectangle is also in the singular, and yet we use "these"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I don't know what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it would have been better for me to put the whole transcript on the ELMO, instead of me mispronouncing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you said in your answer: [In English] "A. Both parties used to take position there, but those were not permanent positions so much as I was able to gather with regards to the situation on the front."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry my friend forgot to read part of the answer actually to the question. I don't mean to keep interrupting, but the answer actually starts two lines earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then you said -- Madam Registrar, says she has found this page of the transcript. Would you want to tender this photo that's on the screen so that she can put this transcript on the page -- on the screen rather? Or do you still want to make markings on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to ask the witness whether his number may be linked to the part of the transcript that I have read out from, and then we can remove that from the screen and return the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, my problem, Mr. Lukic, is we want to know what this man said in the Galic case. And we don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honour. Can this map first be admitted into evidence, and can we then look at the transcript and see if that needs an additional clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D71, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have read the question in line 8, and the answer which starts on line 10. And now I'm going to ask you in very simple terms, was there a building next to the Metalka building which used to hold the positions of the BiH Army? Do you know that? And do you agree with me if I put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, but that was in 1992. After that, the BiH Army could not even dream of entering that building again. In other words, my answer was in respect of the period when I was a BiH Army member between 1992 and 1994, and that was in the Galic case. This incident happened in 1994 when the BiH Army could not cross the Vrbanja bring.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have read out from the case that took place in 2007, the Dragomir Milosevic case. I'm asking you whether you still adhere to your statement that later in the course of the war there were no BiH Army positions in that building?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, I adhere to my statement that after 1992, there were no BiH Army positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this no-man's land during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, I was an army member. There were rumours about this being no-man's land.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the situation later?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know because I did not get involved in any military politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you say this transcript on the screen is from the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. I was the one who initially caused the confusion. I thought it was from the Galic case. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's because my previous question was about the Galic case, and this particular testimony was provided on the 19th of April, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me follow up on your previous answer when you said that you did not get involved in any military issues, did you ever carry out inspections together with members of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: There was one such case, the shelling of Sarajevo airport, and at that time the airport was under UN control. UN invited members of the BiH Army and the Army of Republika Srpska to participate in the investigation. And from the command of the 1st Corps of the BiH Army they called for us, and I never found out why they had insisted on the civilian police getting involved. And that was the only case where all of us worked together, the BiH Army, the Republika Srpska army, and UNPROFOR, and the civilian police. A shell had fallen on the earth embankment, there were no injured or killed, but since that airport was under the control of UNPROFOR, they insisted on the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that representatives of the army of Bosnian Serbs, i.e., of the Bosnian army and the Bosnian Serb authorities insisted on being present during some investigations that were carried out by your service?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I did not know of that. And I knew that there were teams in the police of Republika Srpska trained to perform such duties. And it would have been beneficial and mutually beneficial if we could work together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce P19 -- just a moment, Your Honours. Let's keep this photo on the screen before we do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us -- let me put it this way: Between these buildings or among these four high-rise buildings and the street of Zmaja od Bosne through which the tram ran, there's the Miljacka river; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, the name of the river is Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And also from the Miljacka river to the tram tracks, there was a territory which was under the control of the BiH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And we are looking at that, the low buildings along the tram tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please look at the back and draw an arrow pointing towards the Jewish cemetery, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Impossible. The pen doesn't work. Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is the approximate distance between the Jewish cemetery and Marindvor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: 1500 or 20 [as interpreted] metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that it is an impossible distance for a sharp shooter?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, if you want to hit something -- but what rifle are you talking about? With an optical site, I think it's impossible. From the top of the Jewish cemetery, yes, it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you ask one of your assistants to collect a document from the security there, please. And may I ask that if she can help, because I think the distance is too far from the accused, and the security gentleman are concerned not to leave him alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not used to working in such a large and spacious room.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know in view of the job that you performed when you had contacts with both militaries, do you know that along this stretch between the Miljacka river towards the Holiday Inn hotel, what positions were held by the BiH army members? Were they on any of the buildings?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: In this basement of the school of machine engineering, they had their positions. I know that, and I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When it comes to sharp shooting, are you aware of the term "tunnel"?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. Could this map please be admitted into evidence, the map depicting the arrow that the witness drew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Bolton, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I just have a moment to confer with Mr. Thomas? Sorry, Your Honour, I didn't hear your response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, you may. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. No, I beg your pardon. I was standing here just staring at your head. Be right back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This ugly head?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I just have one or two questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My friend was asking you about the capabilities of a sharp-shooter. I'm just wondering what expertise you have on sharp shooting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Well, I've never used a sniper rifle, an M-76, if that's what you are asking me. So I would not be the relevant person to teach someone how to shoot a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. My friend's question was about the distance that a sharp-shooter was capable or incapable of hitting an object at. And I just want to know on what basis you answered that question, what your expertise is in terms of that area of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Yes, from the characteristics of the M-76 rifle, and if you read the handbook, it tells you at what distance you can achieve the best results. So it would be crazy for someone to use it over a distance of let's say, 2.000 metres, because they could achieve much better results with another kind of weapon. That is why I said that this weapon could not be used for such distances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get the record straight. Sir, at page 78, line 13, did you say you are 76, or were you talking about the M-76? You would be a very handsome, young 76, if you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the M-76 model of rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you were telling us your age. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So I take it, sir, your answer to his question, because I don't I don't think there had been previous mention of the M-76, I'm sure my friend will correct me if I'm wrong, was restricted to the -- or was based on the assumption that this sharp-shooter would have been using an M-76?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: Probably, yes. But what rifle he actually used, he could have used an M-84 in which case he might have achieved certain results.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Another area my friend was asking about was whether there had ever been incidents or occasions when UNPROFOR had asked for access to fragments, and you had indicated only in cases of serious shelling, not sniping. And I'd like to know if you were aware of any cases where their requests for access were denied?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know of a single such case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those are all my questions in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you had wanted to clarify some of the questions from the Milosevic evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think in light of the subsequent questioning and answering that went on, Your Honour, that it's not an area that I need to further follow-up on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Bolton. Thank you very much, sir. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down and travel well back home. Do we need to be in closed session for the witness to leave?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think in order to preserve the image distortion, it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those are all the witnesses we have available for today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, then the Chamber stands adjourned to Monday the 23rd at 9.00 in the morning, courtroom II. Court adjourned.
